catalog_quote: In this section, I describe Abui stress. Phonetically, the stress is characterized by rise in intensity, pitch, and by lengthening. In Abui the stress is assigned in an iambic pattern. In other words, a foot is right-headed and counts at least two morae. The head’s sibling in a right-headed foot counts precisely one mora. The foot system is ‘quantity-sensitive’ which means that any heavy syllable (a syllable with a complex nucleus) projects a foot. Heavy syllables may occur in both word-final and word-medial position. When a foot is projected from a word-medial heavy syllable, the final syllable of the prosodic word is extrametrical. [p. 50] ... Note that a closed syllable in the word kokda ‘younger sibling’ above does not influence the foot pattern. Recall that only bimoraic nuclei project the head of a foot. [p. 52] ... In sum, the Abui metric pattern is iambic. The stress is primarily realized with lengthenin[g], secondarily with raised pitch and finally with increased intensity. Bimoraic syllables attract stress because of their length, which is the only significant characteristic of the stressed syllable. [p. 58] ... Abui prosodic words are stressed following the iambic pattern, with an optional extrametrical syllable. Bimoraic nuclei are heavy and attract stress. [p. 64] ... The extrametricality is triggered by a heavy syllable in penultimate position. As the majority of words have a light syllable in this position, extrametricality is rare. [p. 65]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (563 pp., text layer, the PDF's metadata gives the title 'A grammar of Abui v.7.0'). extracted text of PDF page 72 = printed p. 50 shows the heading '2.5 Stress' followed word for word by the quoted paragraph ('In this section, I describe Abui stress. Phonetically, the stress is characterized by rise in intensity, pitch, and by lengthening. In Abui the stress is assigned in an iambic pattern.. When a foot is projected from a word-medial heavy syllable, the final syllable of the prosodic word is extrametrical.'). I read the whole of 2.5 (pp. 50-65, PDF 72-87): 2.5.1 light monosyllables unstressed in isolation, heavy monosyllables project a foot (ya, lung vs bui, yaa); 2.5.2 iambic feet,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive iambic stress built right-to-left over the prosodic word. Heavy syllables are those with a bimoraic (long-vowel or vowel-sequence) nucleus; closed CVC syllables count as light. In words made only of light syllables the final syllable is stressed (anu 'market' [ʔɑ'nu], kokda [kɔk'dɑ], mahiting 'meat' [mɑhɪ'tɪŋ], malatai [mɑlɑ'tɑɪ]); a heavy syllable attracts stress wherever it stands, so a heavy penult is stressed and the final light syllable is extrametrical (feela 'friend' ['feːlɑ], naana 'older sibling', talaama 'six' [tɑ'laːmɑ]). Conclusion p. 64: 'Abui prosodic words are stressed following the iambic pattern, with an optional extrametrical syllable. Bimoraic nuclei are heavy and attract stress.' Stress is realized primarily by length, then raised pitch, then intensity (p. 58, instrumental Figures 4-13).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; trisyllabic words are parsed into two feet in the bracketed grids of (103), p. 64 (e.g. (l)(l *l)), but no secondary stress is marked or mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: Light monosyllables (ya 'water', lung 'door') do not attract stress in isolation but can be stressed as the last member of a prosodic unit (2.5.1, pp. 50-51); heavy monosyllables project a foot. Affixes and clitics are light and do not attract stress, but aspectual clitics form one prosodic word with the verb and take the final stress (tukon [tu'kɔn] vs tukon-i [tukɔ'nɪ], marang=te [mɑrɑŋ'tɛ]) (2.5.6, pp. 62-63). A small number of mono- and disyllabic words carry lexical tone in addition (2.5.4, pp. 58-62: ía 'moon' vs ì-a 'put down'). Under stress /ɛ/ breaks to [ɛɑ] in fast speech (2.5.5). Extrametrical heavy syllables 'also tend to have high pitch' (p. 58).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word (stem plus pronominal prefixes and aspect clitics); words recorded in citation and in a fixed syntactic frame; instrumental figures from single tokens of adult speakers. Describes the Takalelang dialect (Kratochvíl 2007:24).
new_statements.identity_note: Kratochvíl 2007 explicitly describes the Takalelang dialect of Abui (p. 24: 'present work describes the Takalelang dialect'); the language-level glottocode is abui1241 (no separate Glottolog code for Takalelang seen). Stokhof 1984 covers the Ateng Melang dialect, which Kratochvíl notes differs in phoneme inventory.
